en: In the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, the preceding brief preface is now being annotated.
In explaining the preface, it is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the sequence of the Dharma’s emergence; second, clarifying the reason for composing this commentary.
Regarding the first part, the reason for clarifying the sequence at the outset is that since the teaching originated in the Western Land...
First three, then one;
the transmission of the Dharma to the Eastern Land likewise proceeds from the shallow to the deep.
The analogy of entering the sea can clarify this.
The words briefly uttered are contained herein.
Nevertheless, the sequence of the text consists of three parts.
The first four lines describe the origin and source of the teaching's emergence.
Second, from "Furthermore" (*yuan ji*) onwards, it clarifies that the ancient translations were not yet harmonized.
Third, from "Since the Qin dynasty" (*zi Qin*) onwards, it reveals the profound principles and ultimate meaning of the Compassionate One's teachings.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the statement that the Dharma teachings first began to flow to the region of Congzuo (the Western Regions) during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han:
this refers to the Yongping era of Emperor Ming’s reign,
when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan came from the kingdom of Yuezhi and first brought scriptures and images.
It was transmitted to this country from the Snowy Mountains (Tsong-ling).

Because it arrived from the Snowy Mountains, it is said that its initial flow began on the left side of the Tsong. Although the construction of stupas and images had already begun, those who opposed it still persisted.
This marks the beginning.
It is an establishment.
As for "stūpa," it is the Sanskrit term *stūpa*.
This refers to what is called a "temple" (miao). The *Baitong* states:
"A temple is the manifestation of an ancestral image."
This refers to enshrining the likeness of one's ancestors.
The new [translation] calls it a *stūpa*.
This is translated as "highly exalted.
"Image" (*xiàng*) means "resemblance.
It refers to carving, engraving, painting, or writing the physical form and demeanor of the Buddha.
"Obstructed" (zǔ) means to be partitioned;
it conveys the sense of not yet being penetrated.
This refers to the fact that while the holy teachings first began to flow, the sentiments of ordinary people remained long obscured.
Since it was truly difficult to transmit the profound essence and inspire confidence immediately,
he first established stupas and images and translated the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*,
so that people would know the existence of cause and effect and where to focus their veneration; this was a gradual means for the transmission of the Dharma.
Since this was the beginning of the construction of stupas and images, it is said to be "the initial establishment.
Because the translations and transmissions had not yet spread widely, it is said to be "still obstructed.
Thus, the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Marvels in the Book of Zhou) states:
The World-Honored One appeared in India, the Middle Kingdom.
He was born in the city of Kapilavastu;
at the time of his birth, the earth shook in six ways, the rivers overflowed, and the wells and springs all surged to the brim.
Light of five colors entered and penetrated the Taiwei Palace and pervaded this land.
This auspicious sign occurred during the twenty-fourth year, the Jia-yin year, since King Zhou ascended the throne.
King Zhao said,
"How does he stand in the world? Su You replied:
Now, more than a thousand years later, as the teachings have spread to both this side and that,
[the inscription] was engraved upon stone and buried before the Heavenly Shrine in the Southern Suburb.
Twenty-seven years have passed since then.
King Zhao passed away.
King Mu ascended the throne.
It was the year Ren-shen, the fifty-second year of his reign.
The earth shook in six ways;
all rivers flowed backward;
and black clouds rose up on all sides.
A malevolent beast roared;
in the west there was white.
King Mu, finding it strange and extraordinary, questioned [the sages].
The Grand Official Hu Du replied,
"This is the sign of the passing into nirvana of the Sage of the Western Land.
King Mu said:
"I have always feared that this man would annex our country;
now that he has been extinguished,
what cause for anxiety remains for me?"

From the twenty-seventh year of King Zhao’s reign to the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign, a total of seventy-nine years passed while the World-Honored One remained in the world before finally entering parinirvāṇa.
The *Dàtáng nèidiǎn lù* states:
The origins of the transmission of the teachings trace back to the Zhou dynasty of the Ji clan; the authentic traces of the Qin period were nearly extinguished.

It was during this interval that Liu Xiang collated the books, and Buddhist scriptures were occasionally found within the celestial archives. Based on these, they were compared and verified until the era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
Now, to describe the beginning of the Restoration:
during the seventh year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Han, he dreamed at night of a golden man in the courtyard of the palace hall,
whereupon an assembly was convened for deliberation.
Fu Yi respectfully replied:
"Your servant has heard that in the West there is a Sage,
whose name is Buddha."
"Your Majesty’s vision must surely be correct. Thereupon,
he dispatched eleven persons, including the Court Gentleman Qin Jing and the Doctor Wang Dao,
to travel to India.
In the country of Yuezhi, they invited Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan;
having transcribed the scriptures and images, they loaded them onto white horses and arrived back in Luoyang in the tenth year of the Yongping era.
The Baima Monastery was established,
and from this point the Buddha-dharma flourished in China; thus,
the two masters, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, were the foremost monks in the land of Han.
The image he brought was the first of its kind;
the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* he translated was the progenitor of all sutras;
and the establishment of the Baima Monastery was the precursor of all monasteries.
Furthermore, when the assembly of monks traveled to Wu, they obtained śarīra relics;
from this occasion, the stupa was constructed.
This was the beginning of stupas.
The preceding section concludes the account of the origins and emergence of the teachings.
From here begins the second part, clarifying that the ancient translations were not yet harmonized, including those first introduced and propagated during the Wei and Jin dynasties.
There were four sites in Wei:
namely, the eastern, western, northern, and southern.
The eastern Wei was when Cao Pi, the son of Cao Cao, established the capital at Luoyang.
Later Wei: Shao Ba Gui and others ruled from Pingyang.
Eastern Wei: Prince Dan of Qinghe and others ruled from Ye.
Western Wei: Yuwen Tai and others ruled from Chang’an.
"Jin" refers to the aforementioned Wei.
There were two Jin dynasties;
the Western Jin was ruled by Sima Yan and others, with their capital at Pingyang.
Wang Rui and others of the Eastern Jin established their capital at Ye;
what is now referred to as the Western Jin was the founder.
"Founder" (chuàng) means the beginning.
"Qi" (to open) means to initiate.
"Xuān" (to proclaim) refers to expounding and preaching.
"Chuán" (to transmit) refers to transmitting and penetrating.
That which is called a "vow" means that one’s own mouth articulates what the mind intends to proclaim;

it flows forth with perfect penetration, unattached to any single person, and is transmitted as a communication. As for the various sutras produced through this transmission, there are those whose phrasing is sparse and whose principles are obscure.
"Remote" means distant.
"Obstructed difficulty" (蹇難) is as explained in the *Fayie* (法業):
it refers to the human perspective and the celestial perspective regarding human principles.
Although various [commentators] have erred regarding this phrasing, it is somewhat obscure in its wording.
For instance, in the translation of this sutra, it says:
"The mark of non-coming is the coming of humiliation."
To regard the non-perception of marks as the perception of marks is a statement that,
while verbally refined, errs regarding the principle;
this is the establishment of the principle.
In all cases, the phrasing is coarse and rustic, and the reasoning is stilted and difficult;
whether in style or substance, they do not accord with the Sage’s mind—this is why it is so said. This is because those who study them have not yet attained integration through the Great Perspective.
"Generally speaking," is the beginning of an exposition;
it is also said to be an indefinite term.
"Integration" (*rong*) means convergence.
"Great Contemplation" (*da guan*) refers to the correct contemplation of the Mahāyāna;
it signifies that when objects vanish and the mind is tranquil, there is neither mark nor name.
Because it is nameless, the path of language is cut off;
because it is signless, the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Thus, Master Zhao said:
The mouth wishes to speak, yet words fail;
the mind wishes to contemplate, yet thought vanishes.
This impermanence, suffering, and emptiness are considered minor.
The Middle Way and Right Contemplation are of great importance.
Yet, the translators lacked proficiency in the various regional dialects;
when the Indian monks first arrived, they were not yet conversant in the local vernacular.
This results in the scriptural text having loose phrasing and obstructed reasoning.
These four lines explain the reason for such looseness and difficulty:
because the common vernacular dialects were lacking, the phrasing became loose.
Because the grand perspective has not yet been integrated, the principle remains obstructed.
Since it serves as a subtle guide for the Great Dharma, its merits and faults cannot yet be measured. "Wei" (為) means "to act.
Acting upon the Buddha-dharma proceeds gradually, like the initial overflow of a river's source.
Furthermore, "wei" (to act/undertake) means "yi" (to take up). "Dafǎ" (Great Dharma) refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Its principle is called "great" because it is supreme and unsurpassed;
it is designated as "Dharma" because it serves as the track for generating initial understanding. Thus, it is called "Dharma-illumination."
This Great Dharma can serve as a standard for things, giving rise to correct understanding in the mind.
"Confused" (làn) means to be muddled and mistaken.
"Subtle" (wēi) means minute and shallow.
This clarifies that during the Wei and Jin periods, the transmission of the teachings had not yet been long;
it was like the initial descent of sweet dew, which was still faint.
Regarding the various sutras he translated, what he called "attained" was not yet truly attained, and what he called "lost" was not yet truly lost.
Like a fine jade that illuminates only partially,
or a bright pearl with a slight flaw, it is therefore said that one cannot yet measure his success or failure.

From this third point onward, the principles of the treatise are revealed. "Since the winter of the third year of Hongshi of the Qin dynasty, when Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong" refers to the starting point.
There were four [dynasties] of Qin:
first, the Former Qin (Wang Qin).
First, Emperor Qin Shi Huang and others resided in Yong.
Second, Fu Jian and others of the Former Qin dynasty saw their capital in Chang’an.
Third, Yao Xing and others of the Later Qin dynasty likewise resided in Chang’an.
The four Western Qin were established by the Qifu and Fu peoples at Jincheng;
this refers to both [the Western Qin] and the Later Qin.
Former Qin, under Fu Jian, lasted for sixteen years.
The Grand Historian reported that a "Deity Star" had appeared;
it was prophesied that within the foreign sector of the celestial sphere, a sage would enter to assist the Middle Kingdom, and whoever obtained him would become king.
Consequently, Wang Jian dispatched an envoy to Fu Pi to attack Xiangyang and capture the monk Shi Dao'an.
After Lü Guang had campaigned against Kucha and captured Kumārajīva,
and subsequently Dào'ān entered the Qín territory,
Emperor Jiān joyfully said to his Vice Director Quán Yì:
I do not consider the king of pearls to be precious;
I regard only the wise and virtuous as treasures.
I would not begrudge an army of one hundred thousand to attack Xiangyang for the sake of gaining even one person and a half.
Yi asked, "Who?
Jian replied, "Master An alone is [the full measure]; Cao Zoci is but half.
Jian then ordered Lü Guang to fetch Kumārajīva and saw him off at the Jianzhang Palace.
He said to Guang:
"I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in the Western Regions.
Now, the virtuous and wise are the treasures of a nation."
I have reflected deeply upon this.
If you can capture Qiuci, you may dispatch an express messenger to deliver [the head].
Later, when Juqu Jian attacked the Jin and was defeated, his army was slaughtered by Yao Chang.
This refers to Yao Chang, who established the Later Qin.
When Lü Guang returned and reached Guzang,
he heard that his lord had already passed away.
He subsequently usurped the title;
those outside the pass referred to him as the Later Liang.
Upon Fu Chang’s death, Fu Xing established himself.
In the spring of the third year of Hongshi, a tree bearing plum blossoms grew in the courtyard of the temple;
furthermore, in the Xiaoyao Garden, the chives transformed into wild onions.
All hailed these as auspicious omens.
When Kumārajīva arrived in Yong,
Yao Xing treated him with exceptional courtesy, serving him as National Preceptor and honoring him with the utmost reverence.
He greatly promoted the transformation through the Dharma.
At Cudabao Monastery and Xiaoyao Garden,
three thousand men of great virtue personally engaged in the translation;
the flourishing of the ultimate truth truly depends upon this.
The biography states:
Kumārajīva’s father was the son of a prime minister in India;
his name was Yan and his surname was Jiumoluoluo (Kumāra).
When his grandfather passed away, his father succeeded him as heir. As he traveled east with his uncle, he arrived at Kucha.
The King of Kucha, Bai Chun, had a younger sister whose body bore a red mole;
she was destined to give birth to a son of wisdom.
Various kingdoms sought him in marriage, but he would not accept.
The King then forcibly took Yan-na as his wife, and from her he begot Shi.
At the age of seven, he left the household life and studied the Hīnayāna.
Thirteen, he followed the teacher Śūryamitra to receive instruction.
Maitreya expounded for him the Anavatapta-sūtra;
upon hearing it, he realized the emptiness of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Finding this strange, he asked,
"For what reason does this sutra destroy all dharmas?
The Master then explained to him that because all dharmas are established through causes, they possess no ultimate reality.
Kumārajīva then devoted himself exclusively to the Mahāyāna (fangděng) and received and recited the Three Treatises.
When he first obtained the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (Fàngguāng jīng),
a māra came and obscured the text.
He saw nothing but blank paper.
He made a vow to recite and practice it, and the characters emerged as usual.
Again, he heard a voice from the air saying:
"You are a wise man.
For what reason do you recite this?
Kumārajīva then rebuked him and ordered him to leave.
Furthermore, on the northern border of Kucha, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner who was divinely eloquent and exceptionally brilliant;
he personally struck the king’s drum.
The victor in the debate was about to cut off [Vimalākṣa’s] hand as an apology;
however, Kumārajīva verified the matter through two points of doctrine,
whereupon Vimalākṣa immediately became bewildered and lost his composure.
Furthermore, when his mother took Kumārajīva to Northern India,
there was an arhat named Dharmaghoṣa who saw him and marveled at him.
That is to say, he addressed his mother, saying:
"Guard this well;
if for thirty-five years I do not break the precepts."
In saving sentient beings, he was like Upagupta;
if it were otherwise, he could simply have been considered a peerless talent of his era.
The common people still rely on him as a bridge and a ferry.
When Kumārajīva wished to travel eastward,
his mother said to him,
"The profound teachings of the Vaipulya are about to be widely propagated in China."
"It is solely by your power;
it rests upon your own person without obstruction. What can be done?"
Kumārajīva said:

"The Way of the Mahāsattva benefits others even at the cost of his own life. If the Great Teaching can be spread so as to wash away the ignorance and delusions of the common people, then even if my body must endure the suffering of being cast into a cauldron of boiling oil, I would feel no resentment."
The accounts of his numerous miracles are as extensive as those found in his separate biography.

From this point onward, Master Kumārajīva arrived in Guanzhong; he first translated the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and works pertaining to the Madhyamaka school, such as the *Śata-śāstra*.
"Madhyamaka" refers to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*;
"Gate" refers to the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*;
and "Hundred" refers to the *Śata-śāstra*.

The meaning of the phrase "the sequence of the translation and transmission was clarified" is that [the translator] first refined his understanding of the ultimate truth (*tattva*), and only thereafter retranslated this sutra as well as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and others;
this explains the reason [for doing so].
As for "refining" (*táo*), it refers to the process of shaping clay.
The *Shiji* states that it is a ceramic vessel.
Another interpretation says:
The potter nurtures;
the dyer habituates.
Because the Great Teaching was first transmitted, people had not yet attained faith or realization.

Previously, I translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Śata-śāstra*, in order to nurture right wisdom and lead [practitioners] to the ultimate truth through the purification of habitual tendencies.
My intention was that the transmission and translation would not obscure the fundamental principles; for this reason, I have written this preface.
Regarding the retranslations of this sūtra,
there have been six versions in total throughout its history:
namely, the first, translated by Yan Fotiao of the Later Han dynasty, in two fascicles.
The title is *The Ancient Vimalakīrti Sūtra*,
translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty in three fascicles;
it is also titled *The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Dharma-Door Taught by Vimalakīrti*.
3. Translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty; one fascicle.
Titled *The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door Taught by Vimalakīrti*.
4. Translated by Zhu Jilan of the Western Jin Dynasty; three fascicles.
It is titled the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Translated in five fascicles by Dharma Master Kumārajīva during the Qin dynasty,
it is titled the *Sūtra Spoken by Vimalakīrti*.
Translated by Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty in six fascicles,
it is titled the Vimalakīrti Sūtra;
this is the fifth version, that of Kumārajīva from the Qin Dynasty.

The preceding sutra had been translated four times, and Kumārajīva translated it again; hence it is called a "retranslation. As for the statement that "the phrasing is incisive and the principles reach their consummation without flaw," this means that the wording is elegant and precise, while the principles penetrate the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Master Kang said:
"The text arises beyond the realm of forms, while the principle resides within conditions.
'To arrive' (yi) means to reach."
Having been previously refined by the teachings and attaining a subtle mastery of the sublime truth of the True Doctrine,
he therefore translated this sutra;
its phrasing is exquisite and its principles reach their ultimate depth.
The phrasing is like interlocking hooks and locks,
and the meaning is like a series of linked rings;
because they are not separated by divergent passages, it is said that there is no interval between them.
Now that the profound sutras have been expounded and the great vision has finally been transmitted,
the chanting of them fills the entire realm.
Miraculous responses abound in the biographies:
Samantabhadra dwells within the chambers of those who recite his name,
and Mañjuśrī enters the minds of those who translate his teachings.
Thus, these subtle words have brought great benefit and salvation to many.
From this point, the second section clarifies the reasons for the exposition;
it consists of two parts.
First, the reason for providing this exposition is clarified;
second, the exposition itself is presented.
Within the first [section], there are further two parts.
First, the present loss of the essential meaning is cited as the remote cause;
second, the praise of the ancient sages is cited as the proximate cause.
This is the first [point].
Regarding the saying that "the transmission and practice of the Way have long been lax, and those who study it still look toward heterodox schools":
"Way" refers to the ultimate principle,
while "study" refers to the transmission of texts.
"Zhan" means broad. "Duan" carries the sense of a beginning or thread.
Because it does not accord with principle, it is called a "heterodox end" (yiduan).
I clarify that those who nowadays transmit the scriptures and engage in study are negligent regarding the underlying principles while being preoccupied with mere learning;
they regard profound ultimate truth as true knowledge and a profusion of dharmalakṣaṇas as erudition.
Therefore it is said that one should observe those with heterodox views.
The *Analects* states:
"To devote oneself to heterodox doctrines is harmful."
This refers to having already rectified and governed [the situation].
It means that because the Way of Goodness has a unifying principle, diverse paths lead to the same destination;
whereas heterodox schools do not share this common destination, and therefore they must be rectified. This leads to the flourishing of the Great Source and the manifestation of the Ultimate Truth.
"Rank weeds" refers to noxious grasses.
"Ultimate Reality" (Zhenji) refers to the principle of the ultimate limit of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Rank weeds cause cultivated crops to wither and become defiled.

Frivolous talk and prolixity obscure the True Principle. Second, I lament that while the ancients approached the Truth as being near, those who composed works earlier in Guanzhong used concise language with profound meaning; yet, when these were passed down to later generations, some might be daunted by their brevity and find them difficult to penetrate.
Master Kumārajīva had three thousand disciples;
eight hundred ascended the hall,
and only four entered the inner chamber.
Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong,
and Daoyi were all masters of the profound and subtle True Vehicle whose illustrious reputations have resounded through antiquity;
as they resided in the region of Qin at that time, their compositions are known as the "Works of Guanzhong."

Because the phrasing is concise while the underlying meaning is profound and mysterious, it is said that "the words are brief but the intent is deep. As for the notion that this might be a deficiency on the part of the ancient sages due to the passage of time and the dulling of human cognition:
this is because the contemporary disciples of recent times have become degenerate and their vision has grown shallow.
Out of deference to the words of the ancients, I have been brief and my explanation of the meaning has not been exhaustive.
This is because it was said that the Sage’s era is remote and the nature of consciousness is obscure;
how could there be any omissions or deficiencies in the compositions of the former sages?
The particle "ye" (歟) is an auxiliary used for inquiry.
From this second section onward, there is the formal explanation and exposition,
which consists of three parts.
First, an expression of humility;
second, a record of the reign era;

third, a demonstration of the benefits of the work. I, Li, not deeming myself incompetent or shallow, have ventured to supplement and expand [the text], taking Zao’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* as the primary basis and relying upon Sengsheng’s sub-commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Kui" means to measure and estimate.
Regarding "yong," the *Jia yu* states:
"In his person he lacks the regulations for a careful end; in his speech he lacks words of instruction and rectitude."
Therefore, it is so stated.
"Shallow" follows from a shallow consciousness;
both are expressions of humility.
It supplements with refined detail and expands upon concise statements;
hence it is called "Supplementing and Expanding.
This work on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* follows the commentary of Master Sengzhao.
I have annotated the writings of Master Guangsheng of the Fahua Monastery,
hoping that long-standing delusions may be resolved and that the illustrious traces of Daosheng and Sengzhao may be fully understood,
as detailed in the excerpts provided. Thereafter, one should seek out various commentaries from other sources that accord with these sublime principles.
I have compiled the commentaries of Tiantai and gathered the subtle words of Guanzhong;
with great care, I have sought to preserve the essence so that it remains pertinent and appropriate. Although this is a compilation and not an original composition, [it serves its purpose].
The *Analects* says:
"I transmit but do not create; I trust in and love antiquity.
The meaning is as follows:
In composing this work on the methods of the sages, I have merely followed the numerical accounts and recounted various matters; in the end, I am as ashamed as one who loses his sheep.
Since my explanations are numerous, I feel deep shame for having lost the true principle—just like the man who failed for three years.
Balu’s harboring of doubts refers to the matter of Yang Zhu.

Furthermore, regarding Zhuangzi’s accounts of Cang and Gu, the shepherd, and the inquiry into what they were doing together; as well as the account of Xianxi carrying his books while traveling, asking about gambling for stakes, and the incident involving Ye Youyi—these differ from one another.
Yet, the loss of the sheep is no different [in either case].
Although there are many such explanations, I fear they may deviate from the Sage’s intent.
As for the phrase "the first year of Shangyuan, the year being Kunlai": (Note: *Kunlai* is the Chinese name for the *wuchen* year in the sexagenary cycle.)

The *Erya* states that "zi" (year) is a designation for a year. The *Chūki* (Initial Record), composed at the beginning of the Yongtai era, was further revised during the summer retreat at the Bodhi Dojo;
as it was then the first year [of the reign], it is called the *Chūki*.
"Jì" (Journalist) is an alternative designation for "nián" (year).
In the Yin dynasty, it was called "sì" (sacrifice).
This was revised and finalized during the summer at Bodhi Temple.
Once again presenting this wondrous melody, I am one whose private voice has long been silenced.
It is like a dragon-sword severing objects,
or a phoenix-mirror reflecting images.
May all the nets of doubt for all students be removed, so that the mirror of the Dharma may become ever clearer and the lamp of wisdom shine even more brightly.
"Shu" (庶) means "hope.
The Dharma possesses the capacity to illuminate.
Therefore, it is compared to a mirror;
since there is the principle that the teaching can be transmitted,
it is likened to a lamp.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"It is like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps;
all that was dark becomes bright."
Its illumination never ceases;
that is to say, through cultivation, upholding, exposition, and transmission across vast eons,
the scriptural teachings possess the power to save all beings.

Sentient beings possess the potential for the reversal of the flow [of saṃsāra]. In the second year of the Yongtai era, while I was residing at Zisheng Monastery, during the intervals between transmitting the scriptures, I took up my brush and wrote this in the true script (zhenshu) to supplement its omissions and deficiencies.
How could I dare transmit this as my own maternal legacy?
Shi Zhao’s Preface to the Excerpts on the Meaning [of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*]. This preface is divided into four major sections.
The first generally elucidates the fundamental and the manifested traces.
First, a detailed explanation of the emergence of the teaching;
second, the clarification of the reasons for the retranslation;
third, the elucidation of the purpose of the commentary and sub-commentary.

The reason why the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku) are explained together at the beginning is that the meaning of the fundamental and the manifested runs through all the scriptures; therefore, they are clarified first.
Within this, there are two divisions.
First, the inconceivability of the fundamental and the manifested is clarified;
third, the deluded sentiments and false reckonings are discerned.
Within the first [section], there are again three parts.
First, the names are stated and praised in general;
second, the dharmas are explained individually;
third, the merits and benefits are manifested in summary.
The beginning and middle also have two parts:
first, the designation of the names;
second, the general praise.
Regarding the title *The Sūtra of the Inconceivable Liberation of Vimalakīrti*, it first sets forth the two names: that of the person and that of the dharma.
Although the designation of the person is restricted to this specific sūtra, [the dharma applies more broadly].
Citing the sutras reveals that they accord with all scriptures;
although the texts manifested by the Mahāyāna differ, their principles are identical.
Therefore, the inconceivable does not confine itself to a single teaching.
However, there are generally two aspects to this inconceivable [reality]:
first, the fundamental (hon),
and second, the manifested traces (shaku).
This is explained in detail below.

This heading uses provisional names to manifest the true reality (*dharmatā*). "Gai" (蓋) indicates the initial point of exposition; it refers to the designation for that which exhausts the subtle and reaches the limit of transformation, being wondrously transcendent. This is the explanation.
"Gai" serves as the opening of the various topics.
"Ultimate" (*qióng*) means reaching the limit;
"subtle" (*wēi*) means wondrous.
This refers to manifesting how this sutra exhausts the subtlety of the *dharmakāya* and completes the divine transformations of its responsive traces (*nirmāṇakāya*).
As seen in the "Chapter on Beholding Akṣobhya Buddha," the former contemplates the Tathāgata as the manifest essence (*mūla*),
while the latter takes the Land of Wonderful Joy (*Abhirati*) as its trace (*vyañjana*).
The basis of the Dharma-gate of Non-duality is elucidated in the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulations" and the "Chapter on the Inconceivable";
the other chapters may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the term "sublime and transcendent":
"sublime" means subtle and wondrous;
"transcendent" means surpassing and absolute.
"Cheng" (稱) means "name" or "appellation.
It refers to the subtle and wondrous principle that transcends ordinary realms;
since its essence is both identical to and devoid of marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Name is also precisely namelessness";
thus it is called the "transcendent appellation. "Its purport is profound and mysterious" is a general praise that follows.
It is the essential meaning.
It is profound depth.
"Mysterious" (xuan) means remote.
This is to clarify that the intent of this sutra is profound and far-reaching; it is not something that can be fathomed by words or images.
Because it is without image, it cannot be fathomed through images;
because it is without name, it cannot be expressed through words.
Therefore it is said that "dharmas have no names and dharmas have no forms.
This means that because names are exhausted and forms are transcended, they cannot be fathomed by words or images.
Since principle is devoid of names, it serves as the referent for all things.
Names have no fixed identity because they do not reside in a single name; thus, they cannot be sought through words.
Since the Dharma-body has no form yet manifests as objects for sentient beings, its forms likewise have no fixed identity in any single form.
Therefore, it cannot be measured by means of images.
This refers to establishing characteristics for the sake of fame, which cannot be measured.
This clarifies that both principle and phenomena are inconceivable. That the Way transcends the three emptinesses and is not something deliberated upon by those of the Two Vehicles.
The Way (Dharma) is the true principle.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas must proceed by means of this principle to attain the fruit of Buddhahood;
therefore, it is called the Way.
"Transcending" (*vīta*) means to surpass.
The "three emptinesses" refer to the three gates of liberation of the Hīnayāna, not those of the Mahāyāna;
that is to say, they take the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths as their basis for the three gates of liberation.

Thus, among the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering, one takes the two aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-self (*anātman*) as the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*). Among the four aspects of the Truth of Cessation—
namely, cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*)— one takes them as the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).

The four aspects under the Truth of Suffering—suffering and impermanence—and the four aspects under the Truth of Origination—cause, origination, condition, and production—along with the four aspects under the Truth of the Path—path, method, practice, and deliverance—constituting these ten aspects together, form the door of liberation through non-action (*anabhisamskāra-vimokṣamukha*).
Because the truths differ in the Hīnayāna, the three gates of liberation are distinct;
because the principle is the same in the Mahāyāna, the three emptinesses are not different.
Therefore, the principle of the single characteristic in the Mahāyāna transcends the realm of the three emptinesses of the two vehicles.
Therefore, the two vehicles cannot fathom it. "That which transcends the realm of numerical categories":
"numerical categories" refers to the three aggregates (*skandha*), the four bases (*āyatana*), and so forth;
"realm" means the external sphere.

Because the characteristics of dharmas are void and profound, being free from marks and signless, they are not subsumed within the three categories [of the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements], nor are they transmuted by the four marks [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing].
To transcend the realm of the mind means that what the mind takes as its object is a mark.
Because phenomena are without marks, the mind’s objectification naturally ceases.
Thus Master Zhao said:
"When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail."

The mind desires to take objects as its conditions, yet its deliberations vanish. That which is vast and indistinct (*miaomang*) acts through non-action (*wuwei*) and yet there is nothing it does not do.
"Vast and indistinct" likely takes the meaning of being boundless;
the principle of non-action pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Being stirred, it subsequently penetrates all things; thus there is nothing it does not do.
"Non-doing" (wuwei) is the fundamental essence;
"doing nothing that is not done" is its phenomenal manifestation.
Therefore, Master Sengzhao said:
"How distant is the Way?
It is true in every encounter."
Is the Sage far away?
To embody him is to attain the divine.
From this point, the second section proceeds to clarify the various dharmas individually.
Although the preceding section offered a general praise for how the profundity of principle is difficult to know,
this present section specifically clarifies the manifestation of phenomena so that they are easy to see.
This is divided into four parts.

This means that the teaching of wisdom-body (jñānakāya) subdues [delusion]. Regarding the initial statement, "Thus, the sagely wisdom is without knowing, yet it illuminates all things simultaneously," this clarifies the mind of the Sage.
The phrase "thus then" (*ranze*) is a term used to subtly introduce a point.
Noble wisdom refers to the mind of a noble one;
it is non-conceptual wisdom.
The minds of ordinary beings grasp at signs and engage in conceptualization, and are therefore termed "cognition."
Because the noble wisdom contemplates the ultimate truth as being without marks, it is without cognition.
Furthermore, when the minds of ordinary beings grasp at marks, they can only focus on a single object and are unable to attend to multiple considerations simultaneously;
however, because the noble mind is untainted, its profound discernment becomes even more luminous.
Although there is no cognition, the myriad things are illuminated.
Thus, Master Zhao said:
"Since the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is itself without marks (*animitta*), by what means could noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) know it?"
This reveals that ignorance is [like] the absence of light.
It further states:
"In ultimate truth, there is no trace of rabbits or horses."
Prajñā is a mirror that has no limit to its penetration;
this is the luminous function of knowing all things. That the Dharmakāya is formless yet manifests in diverse forms simultaneously—this clarifies the nature of the Sage’s body.
That which is formless refers to the fundamental nature of the Dharmakāya;
it is the single Dharmakāya common to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
That diverse forms appear in response simultaneously refers to the traces manifested in accordance with sentient beings.
Thus, the physical forms and demeanors of the Tathāgatas in different realms vary accordingly.
Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space."
Manifesting forms in accordance with sentient beings is like the moon in the water;
it is comparable to a single moon rising in the sky appearing simultaneously in ten thousand rivers.
Thus, the following verse says:
Each person sees the World-Honored One before them; this is the sovereign power of the uncommon dharma (*āveṇika-dharma*). Furthermore, the subsequent verse says:

"Countless billions of sentient beings come together to invite the Bodhisattva; at one time he arrives at their homes and transforms them, causing them to turn toward the Buddha-way. As for the phrase, "The subtle resonance is wordless, yet the profound teachings are spread far and wide": it means that while the ultimate principle is beyond verbal expression, its profound influence permeates everywhere.
"Yun" (rhythm) refers to phonetic tones, which are the teachings.
"Xuan" (mysterious) means wondrous.
"Ji" (relics) refers to the scriptural texts. "Mi" (pervasive) means great.
"Propagating" (*bu*) means to spread abroad.
Since the ultimate teaching is wordless yet speaks for the sake of sentient beings, the roots and conditions of those beings differ;
thus, the teachings also vary accordingly.
Because the eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma arise from this, it is said to be "pervasively spread.
Within this that is devoid of names and characteristics, one speaks by means of provisional names and characteristics;
thus, though named all day long, there is no name.
To speak all day long without speaking,
and to name that which is nameless—
this is called *dhāraṇī*.
That which is called "nameless" is termed the "true mark" (dharmatā).
To transform sentient beings by means of this very [mark] is called "established tenet" (siddhānta).
This may be called the Mahāyāna teaching.
The first phrase clarifies the fundamental principle;
the second phrase clarifies the traces of the teaching.
To set the mechanism in motion without guile so that it accords with events:
because the mechanism operates in concealment and responds silently, it is called "setting the mechanism.
Although it responds, it is devoid of intentional mind; therefore, it is said to be "without guile."
It is like a bright mirror: though it has no mind, it is able to reflect whenever a form arrives.
Though the Sage’s mind has no deliberation, its response to things never fails to be appropriate.
The preceding sentence clarifies the ultimate truth.
The second phrase clarifies the response.
This third section generally demonstrates the merit and benefit:
"Thus, it is able to govern and succor all quarters, open up things and accomplish affairs, and bring benefit to manifest throughout the world while remaining non-active in itself."
"Unification" (tǒng) means penetration.
"Multitude" (qún) means many.
"Directions" (fāng) refers to locations.
This means to provide universal access to the ten directions.
"Opening things and accomplishing tasks" means to guide sentient beings so that they understand the duties of spiritual practice.

This is like the eight patiences and eight knowledges of the inner ordinary beings (ārya-prthagjana), which perfect the myriad practices by establishing teachings according to individual capacities, enabling all to receive, practice, and attain their respective supreme benefits.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"May all universally receive and practice [it] so as to obtain its benefits.
Furthermore, it may also be used to guide those in the assembly who are preoccupied with their own affairs; thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
He constantly expounded the Dharma and never engaged in any other affairs.
Furthermore, Sengzhao said:
"To propagate the Way is his primary task; to bring benefit to all under heaven is for him a state of non-action."
Because he manifests for the benefit of sentient beings, it is called "beneficial manifestation.
Because he responds only after being moved [by their conditions], he remains inactive (*anabhisaṃskāra*) with respect to himself.
Following this, the second section clarifies the deluded conceptualizations of afflictive emotions.
Regarding the Chinese text, there are two parts:
first, a specific explanation of false conceptualization;
second, a general conclusion that reveals its falsity.
The phrase "those who are deluded by the initial and intermediate [teachings]" refers collectively to those people who are confused.

This means that because the followers of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings do not penetrate the principle of the True and the Responsive, they cling to the traces and lose sight of the source; thus, their burdens of affliction increase ever further.
Therefore, in this section, the non-characteristics are explained in detail;
the text consists of four parts,
namely the aforementioned wisdom, body, and speech.
